utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-06-90-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, once again. If we could please ask the parties to make their appearances starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Alan Tieger, Laurel Baig and case manager Donna Henry Frijlink for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tieger. For Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Greg Kehoe and Luka Misetic on behalf of General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kehoe. For Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Steven Kay for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kay. Thank you very much, Mr. Kay. And for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, Goran Mikulicic and Nikola Kuzmanovic appearing for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did I hear you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, my mistake. It should be Tomislav Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kay and Mr. Kuzmanovic, this is your first appearance. May I take this opportunity to welcome you to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we proceed, can we just deal with the situation of the health of the accused and let me turn to the accused in this case and verify this they can hear the proceedings in their own language. Starting with you, Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for asking. I understand everything. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cermak. And Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MARKAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everything is just in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's now talk about your health situation, gentlemen, for a moment. Do you have any particular concerns which you would like to raise, starting again with you, Mr. Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for asking. I don't have any health problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm pleased to hear that, Mr. Gotovina. Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my health condition is in good order. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, I'm pleased to hear that. Yes, Mr. Markac. There are some concerns about you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MARKAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my health has been drastically impaired in the last month, but since I have been given new therapy I sincerely hope that it is going to improve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is very sorry to hear your health condition has deteriorated over the last month but we also take solace in the hope that you are under good hands and been taken good care of. Thank you very much, Mr. Markac. Let me now turn to the items on the agenda, the Status Conference which we will -- will be roughly the same as those you discussed yesterday in the Rule 65 ter meeting with the senior legal officer. First of all, I'd like us to state that the last Status Conference in this case was held on the 6th of July. On the 19th of September, Mr. Cermak informed the Trial Chamber as well as the Office of Legal Aid and Detention that he had selected new lead counsel, Mr. Steven Kay, and co-counsel Mr. Andrew Cayley. We have already welcomed Mr. Kay in court. On the 27th, the Deputy Registrar revoked former counsel, Mr. Prodanovic and Ms. Slokovic of their status as legal representatives for Mr. Cermak, and instead admitted Mr. Steven Kay as lead counsel on Mr. Cermak's behalf. As to Mr. Cayley, I understand from my staff that a decision from the Deputy Registrar as counsel is still pending and may be expected as early as maybe in a week or so from today. Mr. Kay, before I ask you whether you feel that you have had an adequate hand-over of the case from Mr. Prodanovic and Ms. Slokovic, let me ask you one thing in regard to your representation in this case. The Chamber notes that you, Mr. Kay, have now been appointed as Defence counsel for the accused Mr. Ivan Cermak. Now, from the public records -- or before I say that let me just say that we have a message here coming from Judge Orie, which I would like to read as it stands. And it goes as follows, he says: "From the public records one can easily ascertain that you have in the past acted as co-counsel with the then-Defence counsel Alphonse Orie in the trial of Dusko Tadic before this very Tribunal." Judge Orie is of the opinion and asked that I inform everyone involved today that the cooperation and association which existed between he and Mr. Kay as co-counsel at the time of the Tadic case is completely unrelated to the present case and so remote in time as to cause him no concern about his ability to perform his duties in a subjectively and objectively impartial manner. If, however, any party to the present case feels otherwise and wishes to act according to Rule 15, then that should be done without delay. And I expect to hear from you within about a week or -- at the very least. Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, we can give you our position now. We don't see any problem now. So that's the position of General Gotovina at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as our Defence team is concerned, we also don't have any problems having Mr. Kehoe [as interpreted] in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is your own position, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I think the statement by Judge Orie was entirely proper in the circumstances. It is in the public domain that many years ago, I think it was 1996 that he and I were co-counsel in the first case at this Tribunal. It is very common as we know in many jurisdictions that members of the Bar go to the Bench, and I have had the experience in my 30 years of practice of appearing in front of many colleagues with whom I had been in cases, even shared rooms with and premises over the years and appeared as counsel in front of them and that has been an entirely proper matter and is not a cause of -- of public concern. It is well-known that this happens, and each party has to do their duty in the interests of justice and that is your function within the criminal process, and I'm grateful for Judge Orie's statement as it is a matter of public record and as well it be mentioned at the start of my engagement in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kay, for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Honourable Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. The transcript reflects that Mr. Mikulicic he has no problem with Mr. Kehoe appearing in this case. You wanted to say Mr. Kay, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I have noticed the same mistake in the transcript. The name I mentioned was Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We just want to make sure that the record reflects the correct position. That's all. Thank you very much. If I may turn back to you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My question to you is whether you feel you have had an adequate hand-over of the case and have you received the case materials from Mr. Prodanovic and Ms. Slokovic so that you can represent the accused Mr. General Cermak in this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have had an adequate hand-over the materials. There are some papers that are still outstanding. I have raised that with previous counsel, and they have told me that they will attend to this matter, and we have been able to conduct an audit of the case papers relating to the Rule 65 ter witness statements. We're still undertaking an audit of the Rule 65 ter exhibits, and we've been able to satisfied ourselves that we have most of the materials and are in fact liaising with the Prosecution in relation to any missing components that there may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do I also have to understand that the hand-over has been so comprehensive as to put you in a position to go forward with the case in the shortest possible time? In other words, not only a handing over of documents but a discussion between you and them of any issues and sticklers that they may have been aware of in the case for you to be in a position to prepare for them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm satisfied with my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then my next question is how long do you anticipate it will take you to be prepared for trial? I have indications of your answer yesterday, but I would like to hear you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My answer is based on these factors: Primarily the amount of exhibits that there are in this case. As I've told the Court, I've just undertaken an audit of the materials. The witness statements are some 160 or so forth Rule 65 ter list for trial. The exhibits under the Rule 65 ter disclosure as exhibits intended to be used for trial amount to 40 gigabytes. I don't know, Your Honour, yet in terms of the Court and Your Honour's knowledge of computing, but I'm told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Completely illiterate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told it's 40 of my old-style computers that I was brought up on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even the old-style computers, I wasn't born yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour has an advantage over me. But it is a considerable amount. I can put it in this terms because this is in lawyer's language: The exhibits I did in a previous case here, the case of Milosevic, the trial exhibits were about 20 gigabytes at the last time I counted them, and that was probably before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slobodan. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was 20 gigabytes of trial exhibits probably before I had the last download of his collection that was to be added to the system. So that does fill me with dread, and I've had some experience of trying to wade my way through this level of materials and it takes a considerable amount of time. So I preface my answer to Your Honour with that information, because it's my duty to be thoroughly prepared, and if I'm not prepared and anyone visits this case later and it's said, well, it was given to you at the time, it's of no satisfaction if I haven't had sufficient time to find important material. In my judgement, that would take one year's worth of preparation, and I told the chief law officer that yesterday, that in my view by the 1st of October next year I would be ready for trial, as I say, based on the amount of material that I've had to deal with at this stage and take an audit of. So Your Honour is going to be faced with this amount of material, apparently, on the basis of the Rule 65 ter exhibit disclosure, and I don't know how that -- the Court is going to be able to deal with that. That may cause a functional problem in the trial process, but certainly in terms of preparation, having to carve my way through that much material I can see it will take a considerable amount of time. As a further factor that we haven't had disclosure of Prosecution expert reports, who are significant witnesses in this case. I primarily refer to two witnesses, one General Pringle, and the other is Mr. Theunens, who is an in-house expert for the Prosecutor. We were told yesterday that his report would be expected round about February of next year. Now, his report is highly significant, because on the basis of what he says as an expert, and again I've had experience of him giving evidence in the other trial of Slobodan Milosevic and know the amount of materials that he is capable of producing, as well as the amount of information that he is capable of producing. We have to send his materials and conclusions to our own expert to get support and help in relation to the opinion evidence that he's giving. That takes time. Finding international experts is not easy. That is why the Prosecution now have their own in-house expert in the form of Mr. Theunens. It was a well-known fact that it was out of convenience and to make it easier for them in the conduct of their case. But the obligation also falls upon us to get a report on what he's telling the Court as a highly significant witness in this case producing very important documents relating to command, military structure, the kind of information that this Court will be basing its judgement upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You understand, Mr. Kay, that if I may just limit myself to the time you say you'll need to prepare, that you will have then to appear before the Secretary-General, because this Tribunal will be no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was going to say it's always a pleasure to appear in front of the Secretary-General, but I haven't had that pleasure yet, nor the Security Council, but in relation to this, I understand the problem, but we are working in the interests of justice, and I know Your Honour is as well, and we have this burden and obligation, and those of us who have to shoulder this responsibility have to ensure we perform our tasks properly so that people look back at this case and say the job that was done was done properly, and that is my prime concern since I am asked as to my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you have told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the comment I just made recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do understand that you may therefore not necessarily get the full year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I give no answer to the question as to how long you will be given. It will all depend on how the case runs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I note Your Honour's comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now, unless anyone has anything to say on what we have been discussing with Mr. Kay, I'd like to move on to the next section. Any comments Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's somewhat in anticipation of some of the other items that will be addressed, Your Honour. I can defer my comments for that time or respond directly to what Mr. Kay just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't want to countermand the suggestion that the expert report will only be coming in February?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll actually address both of the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any comments from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Nothing? Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, you're well aware I am new to the case. I am similar preparation issues. I know we have a team in place already and we're not similarly situated to Mr. Kay and his situation. However, I -- I also need time to get into the case myself. I have not looked at anything other than the publicly filed documents and obviously the indictment, so for myself the time necessary I advised the legal officer yesterday would be at least until mid-summer, July or August of next year for myself just for my own benefit to get up to speed with all the volume of material and documents. So I wanted to make the Court aware of that. Obviously I am differently situated from Mr. Kay given that he is starting entirely from scratch, but I wanted to let the Court know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kuzmanovic. I was going to turn to you but thank you for taking the opportunity to get to the point quicker. You did hear my comments to Mr. Kay. They are equally apposite to you. Thank you. That disposes of the situation of Mr. Kuzmanovic. Now, if we may now turn to the next point on the agenda which relates to counsel for General Gotovina, or am I getting confused? Just a second. I'm sorry. If we can deal with the issues relating to counsel for Mr. Markac. We have dealt with the fact that Mr. Kuzmanovic is also new. I wanted to note with respect to you, Mr. Kuzmanovic, that I understand that your appointment by the registrar is also still pending, but that you were granted permission to attend today's Status Conference. Now, your appointment, as I understand it, is just waiting for your certificate of good standing from your state Supreme Court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's a matter of formality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. It's been ordered. It should be in by the time I get back to the United States, and I will immediately transmit it to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honour, for allowing my appearance today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are most welcome. And you have also been on this case previously as co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On this case I have not, Your Honour. I have been in the Celebici case way back in 1998, and for a while I was in the Herceg-Bosna case for Mr. Stojic. That was about a year and a half ago. I am on the list of approved counsel. I have just not been on this particular case before, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. While we are on counsel for Mr. Markac, I guess an additional item was covered yesterday, that of former counsel Mr. Separovic as investigator. My understanding from the 65 ter Conference is that he is not to be employed as an investigator on General Markac's team. Is that correct or are you able to comment on that Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. After the outcome of events concerning Mr. Separovic, the Defence team for Mr. Markac addressed the Registry to allow Mr. Separovic to participate on our team as an investigator. The Defence team for Mr. Markac hasn't been given a negative answer, and with that we believe that the matter has been dealt with. We informed everybody about that at yesterday's 65 ter Conference, and we would like to drop this issue from now on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we drop it, I would like to get absolute clarity what you mean by the Defence team for Mr. Markac addressed the Registry to allow Mr. Separovic to participate on our team as an investigator. The Defence team for Mr. Markac hasn't been given a negative answer and with that we believe the matter has been dealt with. What is the resolution of the matter, sir? Is he or is he not going to be part of your team whether in the background or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Separovic will not have a formal role on the Defence team for General Markac. We will honour the decision of the Registry, which has established that there is a conflict of interest. We have been given a negative answer, and we will act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mikulicic, but for the sake of absolute abundance, he will have an informal role?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Separovic will not have an informal role on the Defence team for Mr. Markac. However, there will be some time required to hand over the material that he collected in the course of his preparation for the case while he was still on the team, but that will be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying, sir, that he has not handed over the material up to now? For starters, you were co-counsel with him, so whatever material he has you are supposed to have, but even if he has some material that you didn't have, I cannot believe that he has still not handed it over at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have misspoken. Mr. Separovic did hand over the material, but -- I may have misspoken. It is not about Mr. Separovic not having handed over the material from the early days of his preparation for this case, and I'm talking about a period going back to four years ago. He made some notes of his own, and he has promised us that he will go through his notes and that he would inform the Defence team whether his notes might indicate something that needs to be investigated. Otherwise, anything that the Defence team has collected through investigation on the ground is in the possession of the Defence team for General Markac. Nothing has been retained by anybody else. So in that respect there are no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the Chamber can accept that but for whatever outstanding notes that he may have that he's still going through, Mr. Prodanovic [sic] will have nothing whatsoever to do with the Defence of Mr. Markac henceforth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Any -- any comments by anybody on this item before we move on to the next item? Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've just seen on the transcript here my case manager Mr. Mak that it's written down "Prodanovic" and it should be "Separovic".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies. I think I misspoke this time. My apologies. Okay. Anybody else? Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now turn to counsel for General Gotovina. Now, with respect to the Defence for Mr. Gotovina is the status of the alleged conflict of interest of Mr. Kehoe. Let me start off by saying that on the 3rd of October, the Prosecution complied with this Chamber's order to submit to it information on materials in relation to Mr. Kehoe's prior participation, if any, in relation to this case within the OTP. The information and materials were submitted and entitled ex parte and confidential to the Trial Chamber only. I'm saying entitled ex parte advisedly, because I will be asking from Mr. Tieger when I finish here which party has been given the papers. We have been reviewing submission and feel the need at this point to address a few matters with you -- with the parties, and the first point that we'd like to address is which is the party -- the only party that was given the copy of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Chamber, Your Honour, and if it misleadingly indicated -- of course it did in formal terms, I think that was a way of indicating that the documents would be -- would not be going to all the parties, in this case any of the parties, but we're not aware of any particular characterisation that would indicate it was going only to the Court, but I understand how that was confusing and apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not a problem at all, as long as we understand all of us that the Chamber is not a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. May I say if any of the parties, before we carry on with this discussion, feels the need to go into private session, please do say so. I'm not quite sure you may be the one more informed about what may needs to go into private session or not. The Court isn't going to voluntarily go into private session. If any one of you feels like go into private session, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, my only comment is that the difficulty I don't really know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're talking about you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm well aware of that, Judge. I'm just talking about the particular documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll get to that. I'm just saying if you want to talk about those things -- yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make a comment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I said perhaps it would be wise to go into private session first and then you can tell us what it is that we're going to be speaking about and then we can determine whether it will be wise to go into private session on it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can tell you now in public session what it is we -- what we're going to be speaking about. We're going to be speaking not the contents of what I'm going to say, but we're going to say about the documents that has been submitted to the Chamber by the Prosecution that documents the extent, if any, to which Mr. Kehoe has been involved in the investigation of this case while he was working for the OTP. That's -- that's the essence of the motion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is the essence of the motion, Your Honour, but I would point out that I believe at the end of September and again yesterday at the 65 ter Conference we pointed out that it's a little bit awkward for us to be called into a Status Conference to address issues that have been submitted ex parte and to comment on matters that we have not had a chance to even review in preparation so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not going to be asked to comment on those matters, Mr. Misetic. You're running just a little ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's why I suggested maybe private session to be told first --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the parties please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We apologise, madam interpreter. There's a request that the Chamber moves into private session. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Tieger. May I just say in public session now we're now dealing with the question of the status of the contempt investigation. Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm never quite clear on how much information the Court wants us to repeat from the 65 ter conference but perhaps the Court wanted an update on the projected completion date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I did hear, Mr. Tieger. Let me just say, and correct me if I'm misquoting what they told me, the report I get is that you stated that you are not personally involved in the investigation, that you are pushing the team to come up to speed with results. I would like to have indications how soon can we hear, and -- because we want to get that issue off the table as quickly as possible. To say we are pushing the team to come up with results is one thing, but to give time lines is quite another, and I would like to hold you to those time lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. And in the interests of accuracy, I don't think I can say I was pushing the team. I'm outside that -- no, but I did alert them to the Court's concerns and I did speak with the attorney today as I indicated I would, and my understanding is that the projected completion date is the end of November. So approximately one month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Completion of what? Of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can't it be made quicker than that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- that I don't know, and I don't have the details of the investigation, but I think it's fair to say I expressed, during the course of my conversation, the same interest the Court has just expressed, and of course I'll be more than happy to express the Court's concern in the speediest possible resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When the hearing is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The court would appreciate that very much. The matter has been hanging and for some time now, and I didn't think there would be a lot of people to go and talk to about this matter or to get to the source of the problem, but please do express the concern of the Court on the question of urgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I'm not sure whether anybody would like to make any contributions on this. I see Mr. Kehoe is shaking his head. Mr. Kay, you're not even looking my way. And Mr. Mikulicic, you're not making any contribution. Thank you very much. I do think maybe, Mr. Tieger, what would you give as a reasonable time line, you yourself, given the fact that you were going to talk to them? I will not use the word "push," but I would have loved you to push them. I'm trying to push you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- there's a law of physics that applies to that. It just keeps moving forward, and I think it will apply in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I -- if I knew the details of the investigation, that is whether or not it was always -- always should have been very short but it got off to a slow start, or whether or not they uncovered some issues that need to be -- that were unanticipated and need to be more fully fleshed, I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've made your position quite clear. And I will certainly convey that in no uncertain terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to put this time line. I'm going to ask you to come back to court in writing, no later than the 31st of October with a definitive answer from those who are doing the investigation giving you specific time lines and giving you a progress report. That progress report, if you could please file it by the 31st of December [sic] from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I note that the - the transcript says the 31st of December and the Court said October, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I did say October and if it says December, it probably means December 2006. Okay. The tapes have run out. Apparently we need to take a break. Can we take a break until -- until 4.00 and come back at 4.00? Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry about that little delay. And I'm sorry, these are the setbacks of efficiency. My glasses are not here. I guess the next item we were going to look at is the Prosecution's motions under 92 bis, ter, quater, and for protective measures. The Chamber is aware that the Prosecution filed a motion this week seeking that admission of statements of nine witnesses under Rule 92 bis and nine witnesses under Rule 92 quater. And I understand that there may be more such motions in the future. Mr. Tieger, are you able to update us a little bit on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Court's account of the status is quite correct. I presume in asking for the update -- well, I mean the Court has accurately recited the status and the update since the last Status Conference. I also indicated at the 65 ter Conference that I hoped that there would be further identification of witnesses whose testimony is amenable to presentation via 92 bis or certainly 92 ter and I will be alert to those possibilities as we proceed. I don't want to weave in agreed facts throughout the course of that but I think it does play a role in the identification of which witnesses may be appropriate. I will be telling the Court when we address that issue that this has become an increasingly pro-active and aggressive process yielding information that is of considerable benefit in making those assessments. I believe the Court would appreciate it if the parties used the provisions of 92 -- Rule 92 to the greatest extent possibly and we're trying to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Tieger. And what progress, if any, is being made in terms of submitting motions related to protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the -- the pre-trial protective measures, we've largely resolved all those issues. There are only two additional witnesses remaining subject to pre-trial protective measures protection. We lifted the protections for Witnesses P13 and P15 yesterday. At least we advised the Senior Legal Officer that we would be doing so with the Court's permission based on the fact that we were now in a position -- that the conditions which had pertained earlier and upon which the Court granted the protective measures no longer applied and we were in a position to disclose the information to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Tieger. Now, the one or two that might still be outstanding, do you have any idea how soon that could be for protective measures? I'm sorry, I -- I might have misheard. I thought you said that there were maybe one or two -- thank you so much. I thought you said there may be one or two outstanding for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have focused on those two witnesses. I believe we will be able to resolve that one way or another in reasonably short order. It's certainly our intention to do that. So we don't -- don't want that issue to linger any longer than necessary, but because of the circumstances applying to those witnesses it's -- it involves a somewhat continued effort and process but we'll attend directly to that question in -- virtually immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know the Chamber sort of likes time lines. Are you able to give?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I can certainly -- may I do the same thing the Court suggested within a similar problem earlier, and that is at least commit to reporting to the Court within two weeks? I don't know that it will be resolved by then, but at least we can keep the Court updated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want two weeks for this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want two weeks for this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To let the Court know what the status is and -- yes, thank you. If that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So be it. Then 14 days from today if you could file a report, Mr. Tieger. Any other comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, we obviously just received this while we were in transit here. We've taken a quick glance at it and obviously we're going to have comment on some of these motions but we haven't had a chance to fully discuss them, not only between ourselves and the team, but also with other counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've just received the motion and we're working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I guess you will be saying the same thing, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we then move on to the next item, progress on agreed facts. In view of the fact that each accused now has counsel, the efforts on agreed facts should be stepped up significantly. I understand that new counsel being appointed has slowed the progress to some degree and you are now exchanging information, but still I'd like to hear any more information, if there is any, on progress in this regard. Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will tell you that pursuant to Your Honour's instructions and/or orders, we have continued to discuss these matters with the Office of the Prosecutor both on the phone and in personal meetings. Since the last discussion, even prior to that time, there have been letters going back and forth pursuant to Your Honour's instructions. You told us the view on some of the crime based issues and victims, et cetera. We have done that. There are letters going back and forth. I know it's not going to make it to the transcript per se, but I'm handing up -- just a dossier of letters that have gone back and forth between the Gotovina Defence team and the Prosecution on potential stipulated facts. And I will say that the sessions themselves are instructive in many different ways, and one of the most importantly is hashing out what is important to the respective parties. I have taken the liberty after consulting with my co-counsel, Mr. Tieger, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't know Mr. Tieger is your co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the generic sense. As members of the Bar. I took the -- after talking to Mr. Tieger, I forwarded a letter to Mr. Kay as new counsel saying that if -- number one, that Your Honour has instructed us to participate continuously in these agreed facts sessions and, number two, if you want the benefit of our letters back and forth with the Office of the Prosecutor as well as the Office of the Prosecutor's responses, we will gladly do so. Mr. Kay and I haven't seen each other. We had the opportunity to see each other yesterday. He got the letter, and he of course accepted that invitation and as soon as I go back to my office I will forward that correspondence to -- to Mr. Kay, and of course Mr. Kuzmanovic on behalf of Mr. Markac as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Kehoe. Excuse me. Certainly the Court doesn't want to see correspondence between the parties, but -- if that is what you said, I'm not quite sure that's what you said, that you could give them. What the Court would like to see maybe is a -- a joint report on progress. I know you have just given an oral report now, but you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can do that, Judge. I know Your Honour doesn't want to receive the correspondence. I showed that to you just to demonstrate that we have not respectively been sitting on our hands once we got Your Honour's instruction that notwithstanding counsel problems we were to continue to meet on the agreed facts and we'll gladly give you an assessment as to where that is. In all fairness to other counsel, there are issues that impact General Gotovina that don't impact the other accused, and likewise there are other issues that impact the other accused that don't impact General Gotovina, and I'll say that my submissions and my questions to the Office of the Prosecutor, of course, were directed with the defence of General Gotovina in mind. Notwithstanding that, I do believe that the issues that we lay out in the letter will be instructive to fellow counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now that you're on your feet are you in a position to give a time line? Sorry, time line is the buzzword.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Am I in a position to give a time line? No, Your Honour, I'm not, and I say that because I think at this juncture the time line -- and as we move forward, while I can give counsel the benefit of some of the things we've done, in order for us to progress meaningfully into the future other counsel will have to participate as well, because it may simply be that I will agree to a fact that counsel for another accused will not and vice versa. So it's difficult for me to say. I have a better suggestion, Judge, on time line. You give that question to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to give it to you, Mr. Kehoe, on behalf of everybody else to say -- a report on progress thus far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can give you that, Judge, in writing. We can give you a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Do you think that can -- how soon with that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Two weeks? I can give you something in writing by, you know, in a two-week period of time, or -- does that suffice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question of time line would be applicable to everybody? Is Mr. Kehoe speaking on behalf of everybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have not consulted with my co-counsel on this score so I don't really want to speak for their benefit, Judge. I'm just speaking on behalf of General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Would that time line be okay with you, Mr. Kay? I'm not suggesting that you give a report on the -- all the agreed facts, but I'm saying just to give a report on what has been done thus far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dealing with the 92 bis first of all, which is an in-road, so to speak, and a way of dealing with evidence in a shorter form is our first priority to deal with that Prosecution motion. In relation to agreed facts, the -- on the Defence side we all serve three separate interests, and it's very difficult for us to drive such an issue, whereas if the Prosecution was to draft a schedule from which we then started work upon, we could see what it was in relation to their case they were seeking agreement upon and what could be accommodated and not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My assumption was that that kind of schedule would have long been drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the first step in trying to reach agreement on agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I -- as the Court knows, I'm just into it. I certainly haven't come across a document yet, and I've done a -- or had done an audit of what we got, and I haven't seen such a document with the provisions or at least headings of provisions. For our own part we're working upon something that occurred to me of interest for -- for our case, and I was preparing a documentary file in relation to that. But for the whole scope of facts in relation to the context of the case, I haven't seen a schedule yet drawn up that directs my attention in any particular directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any contribution? I don't know if Mr. Mikulicic or Mr. Tieger has anything to say. Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I can only repeat Mr. Kay's words. Mr. Markac's Defence is open for all contacts with the Prosecutor with regard to agreed facts. However, the burden of proof is on the Prosecution, and in this case the Prosecution has to file a submission that would include those facts. We have already started the process, and we are well into that process from the time when before the joinder and indictment. After the joinder indictment, we have not had much progress in arriving at agreed facts. I repeat, we are open for this kind of operation and for contacts in that respect, but the ball is in the Prosecutor's court, and we're awaiting for their proposal for the agreed facts that we might agree with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have anything to say on what has been said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I suspect that the Court's concern is in part that all the parties are expressing goodwill toward reaching agreed facts but that little concrete progress is being made, so let me relate a discussion that all of us had the other day concerning one aspect of the agreed facts process that I believe will yield significant results in terms of expediting the trial process, and that concerned the preparation of -- and I should also say I think this links up closely with the concerns Mr. Kay expressed about immersing himself in the case, becoming familiar with the materials, identifying those materials that are of most significance and so on. So what was discussed was -- and -- was the categorisation of the documentation in the case by their relevant categories. And without going into details, the documents fall into particular categories produced by particular groups that will clearly be the subject of focus in the case and that will be tendered or in the course of the case. We'll be putting those together, looking at them in individual categories. The Prosecution will be identifying for the benefit of the Defence those areas of the documents they're most interested in. The Defence will be identifying any documents that they think for some reason are so unreliable that they shouldn't be admitted into evidence or documents that they think have greater or lesser weight and we'll move on to the next category. In that manner, the parties will do a number of things. First of all, we will have those -- much of the evidence issues out of the way before we begin. Secondly, we'll be identifying the most significant documents and most significant issues in the case, and all parties will be focusing on what the case is really about and what's really in dispute during the course of that process. We also agreed to regular meetings, hopefully in person, but at least by phone in connection with that process. Now, that was preceded by, as Mr. Kehoe indicated, fairly detailed and concrete and specific discussion about crime base related events. Now, I think those are often difficult to resolve in their entirety, although not impossible, but they're certainly possible to narrow and that has been happening. And even when there's not a complete consensus, and there's -- the likelihood of that happening obviously varies, about any particular event, at a minimum, and it's a significant minimum, the parties know what the issues in contention are and therefore know how to lead their evidence much more efficiently. So in fairness, I don't want to be in the position of being the sort of vocal proponent for agreed facts -- for the agreed facts process. I think it's a difficult process. I don't -- I can't cite an example in the past where it's been remarkably effective to the trial process, but I can say I found this one to be considerably different, and the participation of the Defence in this process fulsome and active, and I think this differs from those that have occurred in the past. But again, I just want to underscore that there is -- there has been an agreement on a specific proposal and -- some specific proposals and regular meetings at which those issues would be addressed, and the experience thus far has been that the meetings, even when they don't result in consensus surrounding all of the events in -- of concern, nevertheless narrow the issues and indicate to the parties what the case is really about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree with Mr. Tieger's assessment of some of the things that we've been doing to try to streamline this process. To make Your Honour feel better because I think I know where you're going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm pleased you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Gotovina Defence yesterday, as we indicated yesterday at the 65 ter and told the Prosecution, we have prepared a roster of agreed facts for background facts for things like structure, UN-protected areas which I'm sure Your Honour is familiar with. There will be several hundred of those we will circulate to all the parties within the next seven days but give me a little bit of wiggle room to say within the next 14 days that will be circulated and it'll just be fact, agreed, not agreed and we can move forward and from that perhaps narrow down much of this trial in terms of what we agree on in terms of background. So in addition to everything that Mr. Kehoe has stated, Mr. Tieger had stated regarding what we're doing to narrow the scope of this case, there will also be something on paper circulated where Your Honour at some point in time if you wanted to take a look, you'd be able to take a look at what we've agreed to so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I must say you have done a tremendous job to relieve me. I was almost collapsing. But I think I still, notwithstanding what you've said which I really welcome, I'd like to express a concern from the Bench. But for what you told me, everything I've heard on this point has really not been concrete. I hear we're making arrangements for that, we're meeting, we're writing letters, we're doing what, and I want to say that this point has been raised I can't remember how many Status Conference this is, but from the very first one this point was raised, and the answer has always been we're working at it. Now, if I summarise what I've heard this whole afternoon is still we're working at it, but I'm not quite getting anything concrete from the parties. I'm mindful of you standing, Mr. Tieger, but let me just finish. You know, I say this if you hear -- if you rather what Mr. Kay and Mr. Mikulicic said, we're waiting for an approach from the Prosecution. We can't drive this because we've got different interests and I, at some stage, I interjected when somebody was speaking that a schedule of agreed facts would be the starting point, proposed agreed facts which would be sent to the other parties to say we think we can agree on this. What do you think? And do you have any more to add? I get a sense that we are not at that stage just yet, and I asked myself what is it have we been -- that we have been working at for the whole of this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can say that what we have been doing is following what Your Honour said with regard to the victim and the crime base aspects of this had case, addressing ourselves to the multiple homicides both that have been charged and that are part of the appendix, and boring down into those homicides, so we're not in here trying every aspect of multiple homicide counts. And that is a time intensive process and when we go through those and we have the exchange of letters and then we meet with the Office of the Prosecutor and come to understand what they find significant in this particular homicide count or what we think is lacking in this particular homicide count such as whether or not General Gotovina knew about it, those are very, very instructive issues on several scores. Number one, a broad agreement on exactly what transpired. Number two, highlighting what the areas of difference are, and number three hopefully coming to a point on some of these issues, saying this witness, if called to testify, would say A; this witness, if called to testify would say B. You know, is this a homicide, is this a murder and give that issue to the Trial Chamber. And if it is a murder, is it something that there is vicarious liability under 7(1) and 7(3) if the accused General Gotovina didn't know anything about it. Excuse me. So what we have done is very instructive things, put down agreed facts. We've put forth, concretely, the things we can agree to. The Office of the Prosecutor has responded back as to what they can agree to concretely. So there have been concrete results but I think, Judge, one of the beneficial aspects to these discussions is a fleshing out, if you will, of exactly what the contention is on each individual murder count, which of course, we take very seriously, murder counts in any indictment are very, very serious charges. So we're trying to bore down them, get those facts out and find out, fundamentally, if a murder has taken place whether or not my client General Gotovina knew about it. So I -- I hasten to add that there are concrete issues that are being discussed and agreed on. Now there will be points of departure, but once we highlight those points of departure I do believe it will expedite matters on each individual homicide count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's an improvement on what you told me earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm working on it, Judge. I'm working on it, just developing. But it has the added benefit of being the truth, and I know Your Honour doesn't want to necessarily look at the correspondence --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I recognise you Mr. Kuzmanovic. I'll call you just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I recognise Your Honour doesn't look at the correspondence but I think that my colleague Mr. Tieger will bear out the fact that we have been going back with very concrete facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think it is very proper for any communication between the parties that was not originally copied to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge, I understand. I'm just describing broadly what these letter entail. They entail a discussion of what evidence the Defence has looked at - in this case, the Gotovina, Defence - what statements and what evidence, what medical examiner's reports we've looked at. Is this the exhaustive list? Is there something else out there? Are we missing something? Why? Because we don't want to be in a situation where there is some witness statement that, because of the 40 gigabytes of information, we happen to miss. So I'm trying to be as fulsome as possible. And frankly, Judge, and I've asked a series of questions in these letters and frankly, I've done something in this that I normally wouldn't do - and I'm sure Mr. Kay wouldn't do - in a common law environment which is basically line out a series of questions which would be my cross-examination in a general courtroom setting. So those questions are answered and we attempt to get those questions as opposed to taking that kind of time from the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I obviously have a completely different concept of having to go about that kind of process but thank you very much. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour after the 65 ter yesterday I had a chance to talk at some length with Mr. Tieger about this whole process and getting together and meeting and I'm obviously new to the case and I'm certainly not going to cast any aspersions on anyone, but I know from my experience in the Herceg-Bosna case that, you know, we had six accused in that case, and quite frankly, what I was expecting was a list of proposed agreed facts that I had received from the Prosecutor like I did in that case where all the defendants could get together and sit down and talk about, Gee, this is fact that I can agree to, this is a fact I don't agree to, and then we get together with the Prosecutor and do the same thing. And when I was searching through the materials I didn't see that or find that. And to me, it was a little troubling because I think while what Mr. Kehoe and Mr. Misetic are talking about is productive and valuable, I think it takes a heck of a lot more time and had there been a list of proposed facts, obviously we could have talked about that and discussed that much more easily, even by phone, than it is getting together every couple of weeks and talking for several hours about what facts we can or can't agree to. So you know every case has a different methodology and I understand that but what I was expecting was a list of facts that we could all sit down and talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you obviously practised in the same division as I; that's what I was expecting. But we hear that. Okay. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have heard what the court has said in his general expectations of how an agreed facts process can proceed. That is the way the agreed facts process has been attempted in the past in other cases and in this case, when agreed facts were submitted by the Prosecution in 2005 and 2006 with roughly the same results that I think have been achieved in other cases, which are minimal. Now, I'm not disparaging that process completely because we're still attempting do that, but because of that experience we are trying, in addition, to broaden the process in the manner I described which I think will yield very significant results, particularly in this context where there are new counsel in the case and can benefit from this focusing -- from this focusing on the documentation at -- and narrowing of the issues in dispute in that way. There are a number of ways of expediting the trial. I think in the past trying to get to an agreement on facts has been problematic for a variety of reasons, but identifying the issues that are really in dispute has considerable benefit and is much less contentious and much less difficult to do, and -- and has an enormous benefit in -- in terms of time. So we're trying it from both ends when given the experience that the conventional approach and understandable approach I think has rarely been successful in the past and I don't think has the cost benefit that I believe we're going to achieve from the broadening -- broadened aspects of this process that we're implementing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Let's not go much further in that. You gave -- Mr. Kehoe asked for a time line of two weeks on this point to give something. Do you still stand by that? Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I believe I was the one who said that within two weeks I would circulate the proposed agreed facts on background information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Can we leave it at that. The next item then concerns disclosure of expert reports by the Prosecution. This item was requested by the Gotovina Defence. Mr. Tieger, at the last Status Conference you told the Chamber about your difficulty in obtaining information from archived sources, and you even appeared to suggest that the Chamber impose a deadline on you. The Chamber is prepared to do that, especially when I have learned that you don't expect to have disclosure of some reports until December or even February.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect to the comments earlier by Mr. Kay, he focused I think appropriately on the report of Mr. Theunens, based on his experience as being one that would involve the largest amount of documentation. For that reason, I indicated to the senior legal officer at the 65 ter Conference that, notwithstanding our ongoing efforts to obtain documents and notwithstanding the fact that some documents are still being processed, that is, they have and been sent and received, they're being translated and we're in the process of analysing them, that we would submit the -- Mr. Theunens' report by the -- by mid-December, by December 14th. I thought that one needed priority irrespective of any continuing efforts to obtain documentation. I also alluded to two other reports, the report of General Pringle is not going to be as voluminous, is going to address issues that he has addressed previously and that are largely contained in previous testimony and previous statements which have been provided to the Defence and do not involve anywhere near the same issues. The report that I believe that raise the most -- or that garnered the most attention at the 65 ter Conference was the report related to artillery. I related to my learned colleagues and to the senior legal officer the efforts to obtain that documentation. That was actually to some extent the subject of our -- the previous discussions in court, but I accept that notwithstanding those efforts and the desire to have as much of the documentation for the benefit of that report, that there's a balance between trying to achieve, both for our benefit and the benefit of all parties and the benefit of the Court, a report that's informed by the greatest possible information, a need to get the information or the report to the parties in sufficient time for their -- for them to prepare. And I have attempted to balance that accordingly. I submit that we were not in jeopardy and still are not of prejudicing the Defence's rights in connection with the time to prepare, if necessary, the expert's report, again, which will not be of great volume, nothing compared to Mr. Theunens' report, but the expert's testimony can be deferred to the latter part of the presentation of the Prosecution's case providing, by any reasonable estimate, quite a number of months for the Defence to prepare. So when I indicated a February deadline for the latter two reports, it was in light of a number of factors. I think the very reasonable and understandable desire by the Prosecution to have as much of the military documentation available to it balanced against the time necessary for the Defence to prepare and in consideration of the relatively lengths of those reports which do not compare to the volume of material that is expected from Mr. Theunens' report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I would like to remind you of what Mr. Kay said a little earlier about getting those experts reports, looking for their own experts, giving those reports to the experts for them to help them go through the material and advise them on how to go with the case, so given that background, I would like to say that notwithstanding your undertaking to lead this evidence a little later in the trial, the sooner they get the documentation the better, and I -- I am a little worried because when you began to address this point, you talked of the Theunens report coming in December. Now latterly you say February, indeed, even yesterday, from the report I get, December and February were mentioned, but you also said that the Pringle report is not a voluminous report and in fact it's a report from -- it's something that he has done before. Is there any reason we can't put an earlier time line for that? And perhaps even the artillery report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two matters, Your Honour. First of all, I wasn't slipping from December to February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With Mr. Theunens' report. I was moving from his report, for which I gave the December deadline, to the other two reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And insofar as the other two reports are concerned with General Pringle's report it is dependent upon his schedule. That's -- and I will do my -- I certainly will do my best to see if that can't be expedited. I -- no one would be happier than me at this point to see that happen. And with Colonel Konings's report, I think I have to abandon my hope and expectation -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: About what report? Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Konings. The artillery report you were talking about, Your Honour. I'm sorry I didn't identify that more clearly. I agree it's time to abandon the hope or expectation that the documentation I was seeking will be available for his report and move forward to have a report prepared as quickly as possible so we can get it to the Defence. So I'm not linking that any longer to the obtaining of the documents. I think it was completely understandable and appropriate up to a point, but it's -- now we're coming sufficiently close to that I -- that we have to move forward even irrespective of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What would the time line be if you de-link it from --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was the February date I gave Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: February is the delinked time line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will do my best to see if it can't be done earlier. I want to do that. And should the length of the report or complexity of the report cause problems for the Defence, as I say, we're -- we'll be obliged, I think, to move his testimony to the latter part of the case. In addition, this will not be a circumstance where the Defence is operating in a vacuum. As I mentioned, and I think I indicated that some of these issues were linked to the agreed facts process, we're talking about a process in which there is a very fulsome exchange, in which the parties are talking about what's at issue, what the case is about, what the controversy is or isn't. And so issues -- many of the issues and certainly not all that are relevant to that preparation will be addressed during that process and will augment the preparation of the case for all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose enough said on the topic unless anybody has any -- yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to point out the importance of the artillery report from our perspective and the de-linkage of that report from outstanding issues with the Croatian government. I will state again and summarise what I said yesterday, but I think it's important to say it in open court as well. Might -- one of the big charges allegedly against my client is the shelling of Knin. We have pending motions which I'm sure we'll get to on the agenda items below regarding that charge and whether or not it exists in the indictment in the first place. The artillery report, of course, is contingent upon a finding by the Trial Chamber that in fact it exists in the indictment. Our position, as you know, is that it is not currently charged in the indictment and therefore there would be no need for an expert artillery report to support a charge that is not in the indictment. Nevertheless we have to prepare for trial as if the charge is in the indictment. What our concern was yesterday remains our concern today and I appreciate Mr. Tieger decoupling the issue of outstanding document requests to the Croatian government but nevertheless whatever the evidence is that supports the position that they have charged it should be sufficient evidence to have Mr. Konings as early as next week receive that information and begin to prepare his report. As it stands now on the current schedule, even up to the next Status Conference, we still won't have an expert report because the time line is now into February. It may be, and we can work around making arrangements for calling that witness to testify at the end of the Prosecution case et cetera, however, it is an important point, given the pending motions that are outstanding, given the fact that these allegations, I should say, have been made in the press and repeatedly that General Gotovina excessively shelled Knin and we're hearing today that an expert report can't be prepared two and a half years into his incarceration, or two plus years into his incarceration. It is a concern for us and we -- it is our position that General Gotovina is sitting in a detention unit on one of these types of allegations and there should be no reason on the basis of the material that is currently in evidence, if it is, in fact, charged to have the expert report prepared. Given the importance of that allegation to General Gotovina and his Defence, it's not something that we want at the end of the discovery phase or on the eve of trial to have to scramble to address. And so to the extent that the Court can assist us in getting this evidence as quickly as possible so we know what the case is to be responded to, the more efficiently we can prepare for trial, and obviously to the extent it's relevant to the pending motions, it also would be useful to have such a report. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Tieger, I hope you heard what Mr. Misetic said. You want to rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I did hear what Mr. Misetic said and that's largely what I said. Move forward as quickly as possible, we're prepared to decouple that issue and move forward on the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tieger. The next item is disclosure to Mr. Kay or to the Cermak Defence. The Cermak Defence requested that the agenda include the following three issues: Disclosure by the Prosecution of outstanding 65 ter witness statements in B/C/S and English; two, disclosure by the Prosecution of all Rule 65 ter exhibits to be used for trial in B/C/S and English; and three, identification by the Prosecution from the Rule 65 ter exhibit list of the exhibits actually intended for use in trial. Is that a correct summary of the items --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- from the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to say anything, Mr. Kay, about that before we ask Mr. Tieger to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Firstly, if I take the Rule 65 witness statements, discussion took place yesterday after the Rule 65 ter Conference. Prosecutor's office were able to look at our document that we supplied them with. There are matters that we did not have which are being attended to. There have been changing ERN numbers. That's a mystery to me as well, Your Honour, as I saw Your Honour look up quizzically. And that has caused a problem in the system. I think our audit has been useful because it's been able to see what gaps there are. For the moment, I'm happy that this is being attended to. My concern within that list is of course the expert witnesses, and we've dealt with that already. I just wanted to add to that that this is also important for cross-examination of other witnesses. The issues that the expert is dealing with is not solely confined to the expert. Often their conclusions are based upon matters that can be clarified in evidence that can affect their eventual testimony. So I do flag this up as being relevant to witness testimony generally, because the expert is basing his opinion on evidence, but he may have been given evidence that existed at a particular state and moment that alters during trial. In relation to the exhibits, we do have a massive problem because there is 40 gigabytes, an enormous amount of material, and it has to be accepted by the Prosecution that not everything is in B/C/S or English, and this when we do not know what exhibits we're going to be dealing with in trial as a -- as a prime form of evidence, if I can put it that way, I can't believe all 40 gigabytes are going to be used in evidence, but the prime evidence, if we're not sure what that is then we have a problem if we've got documents missing in either language. I -- I am working with a Croatian team, Croatian speaking. I'm the international figure on the team, and it's of particular importance that those working with me are able to see documents in their own language. So it -- some cases you can address purely in one field if your team is in one particular language, but if you've got a multinational team it is different. But this is a concern in terms of overall case preparation relevant to the start date of the trial, I would say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can only take that as a ringing endorsement of the broadening of the agreed facts process that I mentioned which will -- which is expected to, intended to, and aimed at achieving just what Mr. Kay mentioned, identifying precisely that. Beyond that, I would simply say that when Mr. Kay says he can't believe that all 40 gigabytes will be introduced into court, that's in part because there's never been a case in the history of the Tribunal in which the entire 65 ter list has been introduced into evidence in court. He knows that's not how it operates. And finally, while I appreciate and we're responding to the concern about the volume of material, 40 gigabytes can be a little bit misleading because that -- the gigabytes depend on how the material is stored, whether there are photographs, whether some of the -- whether some of the documentation is a large single item for which only one portion is necessary, which will be identified during the agreed facts process, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But I do think the nub of the -- of the message from Mr. Kay is the sooner they get the disclosure, the sooner they'll be ready for trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They have the disclosure, Your Honour, and many of the problems that Mr. Kay brought to our attention are problems with his record-keeping and not -- no fault of his, of course, and not in -- as matter of disclosure. Secondly, in terms of the sooner the better, Mr. Kay sent me an e-mail concerning this problem that I received at about 11.00 the night before the UN holiday, and I responded to him - the holiday on Wednesday - and responded to him within 24 hours and were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said the day before I went on holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. No wonder you were surprised. Anyway, the point is we are attempting to respond to his concerns as quickly as possible, and we're -- and we've been doing that essentially from the moment he entered the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. In one sentence are you able to give yourself a time line?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For identifying whether Mr. Kay is in possession of all the disclosure materials?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, yes. Your closing sentence was, and we have been doing -- no, I'm sorry. Wait a minute. Where are you now? The point is we are attempting to respond to his concerns as quickly as possible. Are you able to give a time line for that response to his concerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as I say, Your Honour, I responded initially within 24 hours. Today our case managers were in consultation. My understanding is that that was a productive meeting. I don't have the benefit of the results from that discussion, but no one is letting this issue sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Can we -- can we go over to the next item if nobody has anything else to contribute on this item. The application of 126 bis. You can expect that the Rule will be more strictly enforced in the future with respect to filings. In other words, any replies to responses must be accompanied by a request for leave to reply. And the same thing goes for replies to replies. Likewise, other-named filings such as notices or supplemental submissions must be accompanied by a request for leave to file. There has been what I think is an overuse of replying to replies or filing supplemental submissions, you know, just to get further argument onto the issues, and this delays even the resolution of the issue that may be in the motion. Having said that, does anyone need to say anything on the point? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Everyone takes the point, Your Honour, that's why no one's saying anything. They don't want to reply when not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're speaking on their behalf. Thank you so much. I want to believe that. Then we can quickly pass that item and finally get to pending motions. I think you may have been informed yesterday by the senior legal officer that the Chamber expects to issue two decisions in the near future. One decision will be a combined decision which addresses both the 26 March Gotovina Defence motion pursuant to Rule 73 requesting Pre-Trial Chamber to strike parts of Prosecution's pre-trial briefing, constituting effective amendment of the joinder indictment. That's a very long heading. And the 17th May Prosecution motion to amend the indictment. Those will be dealt with in one decision fairly soon. The other discussion will concern the 7 August Gotovina Defence motion requesting provisional release for Mr. Gotovina. And lest I forget, let me just mention this before we talk about what I've just talked about, the order reinstating provisional release for Messrs. Cermak and Markac has been filed. So after this Status Conference, just for you to take note that that has been filed. Is there any comment on the other issues? Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just, Judge with regard to the provisional release motion we have pending, we also have had a motion pending for an evidentiary hearing on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. That will be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will hear about that, sir. Okay. Anything else? Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Nothing from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kay? Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other thing that any of the parties would like to raise at this Status Conference which maybe was not on the agenda? Starting with you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I say thank you very much to all of you. That brings us to conclusion of the Status Conference. The court stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: at 5.00 p.m.
